summary: This informational document states the problem of localized routing in Proxy Mobile IPv6. Normally all traffic goes through the Local Mobility Anchor, even between two nearby nodes. It describes why and where direct paths between access gateways would help.

plainLanguage.summary: When two phones on the same operator's network talk to each other, their packets still travel to the operator's central server and back. This memo describes the problem of sending those packets directly between the two base stations instead, and lists what a protocol would have to do to make that safe.

questions: route optimization in proxy mobile ipv6
subtitle: Routing data directly between access gateways instead of through a distant anchor.

tldr.problem: In Proxy Mobile IPv6 every packet between two mobile nodes goes through their mobility anchors, even when both nodes are attached to gateways in the same operator's network.
tldr.mechanism: The memo describes what a solution has to do: the network, not the mobile nodes, must detect that a direct path is possible, set up the routing state on the two gateways, keep it through handovers and tear it down again.
tldr.outcome: It is a problem statement, not a protocol. Its output is a list of functional requirements that a later design can be measured against.

today: RFC 6279 is an Informational document from June 2011, and the unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes it and none that updates it. It is a problem statement, so it describes what a localized routing solution must do rather than how to do it.

sections.title: The Problem in One Paragraph
sections.content:
The IETF has specified Proxy Mobile IPv6 (RFC 5213) as the base protocol for network-based localized mobility management. The scope of the base protocol covers the setup and maintenance of a tunnel between a mobile node's Mobile Access Gateway and its selected Local Mobility Anchor. Data packets will always traverse the mobile node's gateway and its anchor, irrespective of the location of the mobile node's remote communication endpoint. Even though a node may be attached to the same gateway, or a different gateway, as its correspondent node within the same provider domain, packets associated with their communication will traverse both nodes' anchors, which can be located topologically far away from the gateways or even in a separate provider domain.

RFC 5213 addresses the need to enable local routing of traffic between two nodes attached to the same gateway, but does not specify the complete procedure to establish such localized routing state on the shared gateway.

The NetLMM Extensions working group has an objective to design a solution for localized routing in PMIPv6. That objective includes the specification of protocol messages and associated protocol operation between PMIPv6 components to support the setup of a direct routing path for data packets between the two gateways, while both hosts receive mobility service according to the PMIPv6 protocol. As a result of localized routing, packets are forwarded between the two gateways without traversing the anchors. In cases where one or both nodes hand over to a different gateway, the localized routing protocol maintains the localized routing path. Relevant protocol interfaces may include the interface between associated gateways, between a gateway and an anchor, and between anchors. The setup of localized routing with correspondent nodes not registered with a PMIPv6 network is out of scope of that solution and of this problem statement.
sections.plainLanguage: PMIPv6 keeps a mobile node's traffic anchored at a server in the operator's core network. Everything a node sends goes there and comes back, even when the node is talking to a machine on the same access network. This memo is about the case where the traffic could simply go from one access gateway to the other.

sections.title: The Vocabulary
sections.content:
The document uses the terminology of RFC 5213 and adds four terms. A Mobile Node is a mobile node without IP mobility support, which is attached to a Mobile Access Gateway and registered with a Local Mobility Anchor according to the PMIPv6 specification. A Correspondent Node is the communication peer of such a mobile node, with or without IP mobility support.

Localized Routing is the result of signalling to set up routing states on the relevant network entities that allow forwarding of data packets between a mobile node and a correspondent node which are attached to gateways sharing the same provider domain, without the intervention of the mobile node's anchor and the correspondent node's anchor in data forwarding. Localized Routing States are the pieces of information for localized routing on the relevant forwarding entities on the optimised data path between the two nodes. Such information includes route entries and tunnel endpoints, and may include further information about the two nodes, such as their Mobile Node Identifier and their assigned Home Network Prefix. A Provider Domain is a network domain in which network components are administered by a single authority, for example the mobile operator.
sections.plainLanguage: Four terms matter here. The mobile node is the device that moves. The correspondent node is who it is talking to. Localized routing means the two talk directly instead of via the anchors. And a provider domain is the part of the network one organisation runs.

sections.title: Why Operators Would Want Local Routing
sections.content:
Mobile IPv6 (RFC 3775) has built-in mechanisms for direct communication between a mobile node and a correspondent node. Mechanisms for route optimisation in Mobile IPv6 cannot be directly applied in PMIPv6: mobile nodes are not involved in mobility signalling and hence cannot perform signalling to set up localized routes. Instead, the solution for localized routing must consider functions in the network to find out whether a localized route is to be used and then control the setup and maintenance of localized routing states accordingly, without any assistance from the mobile node and the correspondent node.

Localized routing is understood in RFC 5213 as an optimisation of traffic between a mobile node and a correspondent node attached to an access link connected to the same gateway. In that case the gateway forwards traffic directly between the two, assuming it is enabled to support the feature through the setting of the EnableMAGLocalRouting flag, and the mobile node's anchor enforces the optimisation. RFC 5213 does not specify how an anchor can enforce the optimisation for such local communication, and maintaining local forwarding between the mobile node and a regular IPv6 correspondent node gets more complex when the mobile node hands over to a different gateway. This document focuses on use cases where both nodes are within a PMIPv6 network and served by an anchor in a domain of anchors.

With localized routing, operators have the possibility of offloading traffic from anchors and from the core network. Establishing a direct path between the two gateways is beneficial for two reasons. First, by limiting the communication to the access nodes, the data traffic traversing the gateway to anchor path can be reduced, which is significant given that the transport network between the access and the core is often the bottleneck in terms of costs and performance. Second, there may be performance benefits for data flows between the two nodes in terms of delay and packet loss, especially when both are attached to the same gateway and the anchor is topologically far away from it. Even when the nodes are attached to different gateways, there could be benefit in limiting the communication to the access network only. Offloading traffic from the anchor also improves the scalability of the anchor, since it is a bottleneck for traffic being forwarded by many gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: Two reasons to want the shortcut. The link between the access network and the operator's core is often the expensive, slow part, so keeping traffic off it saves money and reduces delay. And the anchor has to forward everything, so taking the easy traffic off it lets it handle the rest better.

sections.title: The Use Cases and the Hard Parts
sections.content:
The problem statement focuses on local communication between PMIPv6 managed nodes which attach to gateways sharing the same provider domain. The use cases consider the existence of multiple anchors, and are named by the number of gateways and anchors involved: A11, A12, A21 and A22.

In A11, the mobile node and the correspondent node connect to the same gateway and are registered with the same anchor. The common gateway may forward packets between them directly without forwarding any packet to the anchor. RFC 5213 addresses this use case but does not specify the complete procedure to establish such localized routing state on the shared gateway. In A12, the two connect to the same gateway but are registered with different anchors. The common gateway may still forward packets directly, but potential problems exist in the case where the two anchors differ in their policy for controlling the gateway.

In A21, the correspondent node connects to a different gateway than the mobile node, but both are registered with the same anchor. The result of localized routing should be routing information at both gateways, allowing direct forwarding between them. Because that anchor is the common anchor for both nodes and maintains location information for both, no major race condition and instability in updating the states is expected. In A22, the correspondent node connects to a different gateway and a different anchor. Routing information is again needed at both gateways, but as the location information of the two nodes is maintained at different anchors, both anchors have to be involved in the procedure. In the case of a handover of one or both nodes to a different gateway, non-synchronised control of updating the states may result in race conditions, superfluous signalling and packet loss.

Three general problems follow. Mobile nodes do not participate in mobility management and hence cannot perform binding registration at a correspondent node on their own, so entities in the network infrastructure must take over that role, which means the solution must specify protocol operation between relevant network components such as between a gateway and an anchor. When the two nodes are registered with different anchors, the information needed to set up a localized path, such as the current gateway of each node, is distributed between those anchors, which may complicate the setup and stable maintenance of the states. And if both nodes move and attach to a new access router at the same time, signalling the new location may run into a race condition: as a result of the mobile node's handover, updated information about its location may arrive at the correspondent node's previous gateway while the correspondent node has already moved to a new gateway, and the same applies in the other direction. The protocol solution must deal with such exceptional handover cases efficiently.
sections.plainLanguage: The easy case is two devices behind one gateway and one anchor. The hard cases are when the anchors differ, because then the information needed to build the shortcut is in two places and has to be kept in step. The nastiest case is both devices moving at once, when each one's new location can arrive at the other's old gateway after the fact.

sections.title: What a Solution Has to Do
sections.content:
Several tasks need to be performed by the network infrastructure components before the relevant information for direct communication is discovered and the associated states can be set up. The document summarises the key functions that the PMIPv6-enabled infrastructure has to perform in order to substitute for the mobile nodes in setting up a direct route. These are: detection of the possibility to perform localized routing, which includes looking at a data packet's source and destination address; initiation of a procedure that sets up a localized routing path; discovery of the stateful entities, that is the anchors and/or gateways, that maintain and can provide the relevant information needed to set up the path, such as the routable address of an anchor or gateway where one or both mobile nodes are connected and registered; control in setting up and maintaining the path, for example during a handover, which is also needed to terminate the use of a localized path and delete the associated states, where a trigger for the termination may come from a component unrelated to PMIPv6; and enforcement of administrative policy rules, which allow operators to have further control over the setup of a localized route and enable the possibility of disallowing localized routing, for example to ensure that traffic traverses charging-related functions on the anchor. Explicit authorization of localized routing is discussed in a Diameter document, and mobile-node-specific and operator-specific policy rules can be established on PMIPv6 components during bootstrapping.

IPv4 support adds its own constraints. According to RFC 5844, the basic configuration requirements for supporting IPv4 in PMIPv6 are that anchors and gateways are both IPv4 and IPv6 enabled, and that both have a globally unique IPv6 address configured. Where an anchor and a gateway hold a registration supporting IPv4 home address mobility, they must support appropriate encapsulation of IPv4 packets, and the mobile node's gateway must ensure that the chosen encapsulation mode is supported by the correspondent gateway, since incompatibility causes failure in setting up a localized route. The routing state on the associated gateways must be keyed on the complete IPv4 source and destination address, and because IPv4 addresses from a private address space may overlap, the solution may need extra mechanisms to tag and identify the two nodes uniquely. The transport network between the anchor and the gateway may be based on IPv6 or IPv4, and the version used for localized routing is assumed by configuration to be consistent across all gateways within the associated provider domain.

Roaming adds a boundary. To support localized routing when roaming occurs, the gateways to which the two nodes connect must be within the same provider domain, and each gateway must have a security relationship with the corresponding anchor that holds the registration of the node. Four cases are considered, in which the two gateways and the two anchors are placed in the same or different provider domains. During mobility, the two nodes should remain attached to gateways of the same provider domain to maintain efficient routing of traffic between those gateways.
sections.plainLanguage: The infrastructure has to do five things: notice that a direct route is possible, start setting it up, find the equipment that holds the necessary records, keep the route working through handovers, and obey the operator's rules about when to allow it at all. With IPv4 in the mix, the two ends must also agree on how the packets are wrapped.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A protocol solution for localized routing in a PMIPv6 network must counter unauthorized change of a routing path. In particular, the control plane for localized routing must preclude the blocking or hijacking of mobile nodes' traffic by malicious or compromised network components. A security solution must support suitable mechanisms for authentication of the control plane components of the localized routing functional architecture for both roaming and non-roaming scenarios. Any possibility for Internet hosts to interfere with the localized routing procedure in a malicious manner must be precluded.

Since network entities other than the mobile node and the correspondent node perform the signalling that sets up localized routing, the Mobile IPv6 return routability test (RFC 3775) is not suitable to authenticate associated signalling messages in PMIPv6. Solutions for localized routing in PMIPv6 need to mitigate, or provide sufficient defense against, possible security threats. When PMIPv6 participants are administered within the same domain, infrastructure-based authorization mechanisms such as IPsec may be usable to protect signalling for localized routing.

Existing security associations according to RFC 5213 can be re-used to protect signalling for localized routing on the interface between a gateway and an anchor. In the case where a protocol solution relies on protocol operation between gateways, means for the protection of signalling between those gateways must be provided. The same applies for signalling on a possible protocol interface between two anchors of the same domain.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the shortcut changes where traffic goes, an attacker who could push a routing change could divert a user's traffic. The network has to authenticate the parts that build the shortcut, and it can reuse the security associations PMIPv6 already sets up between a gateway and an anchor. A gateway to gateway link needs its own protection, because PMIPv6 does not create one today.

viz.caption: THE REFERENCE ARCHITECTURE FOR LOCALIZED ROUTING
THE FOUR USE CASES AND WHAT EACH ONE NEEDS

cells: Both nodes on the same gateway, registered with the same anchor
The shared gateway can forward directly; RFC 5213 addresses this but does not give the full procedure
The shared gateway can still forward directly, but the two anchors may differ in their policy for controlling the gateway
Routing state at both gateways; one anchor holds both locations, so no major race is expected
Routing state at both gateways; both anchors must take part, so handovers can race

viz.caption: THE FIVE FUNCTIONS THE NETWORK MUST PERFORM

items.title: Detect the possibility
items.text: Look at a data packet's source and destination address to see whether a direct route could be used.

items.title: Start the setup
items.text: Initiate the procedure that establishes the localized routing path.

items.title: Find the right equipment
items.text: Discover the anchors and gateways that hold the information needed, and their routable addresses.

items.title: Control it
items.text: Set the path up, maintain it during handovers, and tear it down when it should no longer be used.

items.title: Apply policy
items.text: Enforce administrative rules, including refusing to localize a route so that traffic still crosses the anchor's charging functions.
